analysis.one_liner: Bans forcing workers and consumers to sign away their day in court before a dispute happens.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 103 cosponsors and won subcommittee approval by voice vote, but the full House Judiciary Committee never voted on it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal arbitration law so that companies could no longer require employees, consumers, or franchisees to give up their right to go to court as a condition of a job, a credit card, a phone plan, or a franchise. Under today's law, fine-print clauses in those contracts send disputes to private arbitrators chosen under systems paid for by the companies. After this bill, a company and a person could still agree to arbitrate, but only after a dispute actually arose, and a judge — not an arbitrator — would decide whether the agreement was valid.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees, consumers, and franchisees who today sign predispute arbitration clauses as a condition of employment or buying goods and services. The bill's own findings say millions of people must accept these clauses to get a job, medical care, a car, a bank account, or a credit card, often without realizing they have given up their right to a judge or jury [S3]. It would let civil-rights and consumer-protection claims be heard in public court, where decisions are written and reviewable, rather than in private arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any predispute arbitration agreement from being enforced for employment, consumer, or franchise disputes, or for claims under civil-rights and consumer-protection statutes [S2] [S3].
Puts the decision about whether an arbitration agreement is valid in the hands of a court applying federal law, rather than the arbitrator hired under the contract [S2] [S3].
Keeps arbitration available for union members by exempting collective bargaining agreements, where arbitration is negotiated rather than imposed in fine print [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that use predispute arbitration clauses — employers, banks, credit card issuers, phone companies, nursing homes, and franchisors — would face employment, consumer, and civil-rights claims in open court, where proceedings are public and outcomes can set legal precedent. Businesses argue this raises litigation costs and removes a faster, cheaper dispute channel.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for some disputes, and critics of the bill argued that eliminating predispute clauses would push more cases into an expensive, slow court system whose costs could be passed on to consumers through prices [S3].

The bill does not make arbitration illegal; people can still choose it after a dispute arises. Its entire effect depends on the premise that a pre-emptive, fine-print waiver is not a genuine choice, which companies dispute [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would restore access to the courts for millions of people whose employment and consumer contracts currently waive that access in advance, at the cost of more litigation for companies that have relied on private, non-appealable arbitration. The trade-off is real for businesses, but the bill leaves genuinely negotiated arbitration — including union contracts and post-dispute agreements — untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, a subcommittee held hearings and sent it to the full committee by voice vote in July 2008, but the full committee never voted and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Hank Johnson of Georgia introduced the bill on July 12, 2007, with eight original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1] [S5].
It gathered 103 cosponsors, 98 Democrats and 5 Republicans [S4].
The Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee held a hearing in October 2007 and a markup in July 2008, forwarding the bill to the full committee by voice vote [S5].
The full Judiciary Committee never took a vote, and the bill was never brought to the House floor before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that require predispute arbitration clauses kept the ability to route employment, consumer, and civil-rights disputes into private arbitration, since the bill never became law. The private arbitration industry kept its corporate client base as well.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies relying on mandatory arbitration clauses

for.name: Hank Johnson Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Arbitration Fairness Act of 2007 and recruited cosponsors across the Congress.

for.name: 98 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority-caucus support.

for.name: 5 of 199 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small bipartisan minority.

for.name: Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing in October 2007, marked the bill up in July 2008, and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote.

against.name: John Conyers Jr.
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a full-committee markup or vote on the bill after the subcommittee forwarded it, and the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship ran 98 Democrats to 5 Republicans, so support was overwhelmingly but not entirely from one party; the bill never drew a roll-call vote that would show the full chamber's split [S4].

industries.industry: Corporations using mandatory arbitration clauses (employers, banks, credit card issuers, phone and nursing-home companies)
industries.note: The bill would strip their ability to send employment, consumer, and civil-rights disputes to private arbitration chosen in fine print, exposing them to public court proceedings instead. Their cost of litigation is the public's regained access to the courts [S2] [S3].
Franchise disputes are expressly covered, so franchisors could no longer require franchisees to pre-waive court access in the franchise contract [S3].

The bill's findings describe arbitration firms as dependent on lucrative repeat business from the corporations that decide whether to hire them; ending mandatory predispute clauses would cut that revenue stream. Firms could still handle genuinely negotiated, post-dispute arbitration [S3].

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' attorneys handling consumer and employment cases
industries.note: Restoring court access for these claims expands the pool of cases that can be litigated, including class and civil-rights suits that arbitration clauses often bar [S3].
